gap: No result ChatGPT got says that 'hot-swappable' on the low-profile picks only lets you change to switches from that board's own low-profile family (NuPhy lists the Air75 V3's switch type as 'Low-profile 3.0'; Digital Trends says of the Flow 2 that 'Hot-swappable doesn't mean every mechanical switch you find online will fit'), so a typist must pick the switch feel when buying instead of counting on the wider MX switch market later.
standout_why: I compared against the two cited rivals, RTINGS 'Best Keyboards For Typing' and Tom's Guide 'best mechanical keyboards', plus ChatGPT's own answer. Neither rival page returned its article text to my fetcher; I got only navigation, so I can't fully rule out that they mention socket families. ChatGPT's answer only says 'customizable switches' for the Q1 Max and 'hot-swappable options' for the K8 Max. It never says which switches each board's sockets accept, or that its two low-profile picks (Air75 V3, Halo75 V2 is full height) shut out standard MX switches. The score is 2, not 3: the mechanism matters only to shoppers who plan to try other switches, and I couldn't source the MX-side half of the comparison from Keychron.
decides: This confirms how the pick splits rather than overturning it. A shopper who wants to try tactile vs linear vs silent switches after buying should get a full-height MX-socket board like the Keychron Q1 Max. A shopper set on low-profile (NuPhy Air75 V3, Lofree Flow 2 84 or Flow Lite 2 84) should choose the stock switch (Red, Brown or Blush; Surfer, Pulse or Void) at checkout, because later swaps are limited to that maker's low-profile family. The page should put this sentence next to the 'hot-swap' cells.
